title: YOU WANT JESUS AS YOUR SAVIOR… BUT DO YOU REALLY WANT HIM AS YOUR LORD?
paragraphs: YOU WANT JESUS AS YOUR SAVIOR… BUT DO YOU REALLY WANT HIM AS YOUR LORD?

You want His blood to cover your sins. You want His grace to rescue your soul. You want His promises over your future. But what happens when the same Jesus who offers you forgiveness asks you to surrender the very thing you refuse to let go?
There is a frightening possibility that many churchgoing people rarely consider.
You can know the worship songs. You can quote the Bible. You can raise your hands when the music reaches its highest point.
And still spend most of your life resisting His authority.
Not because you have never heard His name.
But because you have learned how to speak about surrender without actually surrendering.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this:
The Jesus you call upon to save you is the same Jesus who calls you to follow Him.
You cannot rewrite His invitation to make room for the sins you have already decided to protect.
Read that again.

Because somewhere between wanting heaven and avoiding hell, between Sunday worship and Monday compromise, between asking God for blessings and resisting His correction, we may have forgotten something Jesus never concealed.
He did not simply say, “Admire Me.”
He said, “Follow Me.”
And following Him changes everything.
Imagine standing before Jesus.
Not before a preacher. Not before a congregation. Not before the people who know your Christian reputation.
Before Jesus Himself.

The One who saw every private decision. Every secret conversation. Every compromise you justified. Every conviction you silenced. Every opportunity to repent that you postponed because you thought there would always be another tomorrow.
You begin to speak.
“Lord, I believed in You.”
“Lord, I went to church.”
“Lord, I shared Your Word.”
“Lord, I did things in Your name.”
Then you remember something He once said.
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” — Matthew 7:21, KJV
Jesus continues in Matthew 7:22–23 by describing people who appeal to impressive religious works, only to hear Him declare that He never knew them.
Those words should disturb anyone who has mistaken religious activity for a living relationship with Christ.
But notice what Jesus is exposing.
He is not condemning a struggling believer who hates their sin and keeps returning to Him in repentance.
He is exposing the terrifying emptiness of a religious profession that exists without genuine allegiance to God.
The issue is not whether you have ever stumbled.
The issue is whether you have made peace with living apart from the One you call Lord.
There is a difference between falling into sin and building a home inside it.
A difference between struggling against temptation and defending it.
A difference between crying out for mercy and demanding that God approve what He has forbidden.
And that difference matters.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make sinners feel better about remaining unchanged.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To reconcile us to the Father.
To give us new life.
And yes, to transform the hearts that once resisted Him.
In Luke 6:46, Jesus asks a question that cuts through centuries of religious performance:
“Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — KJV
The original Greek is even more striking:
Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;
Ti de me kaleite, Kyrie kyrie, kai ou poieite ha legō?
The sense is direct: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?”
The Greek word Κύριε (Kyrie) is the form of address from κύριος (kyrios), meaning “lord” or “master,” and, depending on context, a title of divine authority.
Jesus is confronting a contradiction between what people call Him and how they respond to His words.
He is not asking for a more emotional worship service.
He is asking why the lips acknowledge an authority the life refuses to obey.
And suddenly, the question becomes painfully personal.
What if the biggest obstacle in your walk with God is not that you do not know what He wants?
What if you know…
But you do not want to give it up?
That relationship you know is drawing you away from Christ.
That bitterness you have rehearsed so often that forgiveness now feels like betrayal.
That private habit you keep promising to abandon.
That dishonest business decision you excuse because everyone else does it.
That pride that would rather lose a relationship than admit wrongdoing.
That secret life you carefully separate from your public testimony.
You love hearing that Jesus forgives.
But when He confronts what is destroying you, something inside begins negotiating.
“Lord, anything but this.”
“I will serve You, but please do not touch that relationship.”
“I will follow You, but let me keep this one habit.”
“I will obey You, but not if it costs my reputation.”
“I will surrender, but not yet.”
And perhaps this is where the deepest spiritual battle begins.
Not between you and the world.
But between your will and the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
There is a man in Scripture whose story should make every comfortable Christian uncomfortable.
He came to Jesus with an extraordinary question.
“What shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?” — Mark 10:17, KJV
He was serious enough to approach Jesus. Morally respectable enough to speak of keeping the commandments. Wealthy enough to possess much.
By ordinary standards, he seemed like someone who had everything going for him.
But Jesus saw what no one else could see.
Mark 10:21 says:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him…”
Do not miss those words.
Jesus loved him.
Before Jesus exposed his attachment, He loved him.
Before He called him to a costly decision, He loved him.
Before the man walked away grieving, Jesus loved him.
Then Jesus told him to sell what he possessed, give to the poor, and follow Him.
This was not a universal command that every Christian must sell every possession to be saved. It was a specific confrontation with the attachment that ruled this man's heart.
Jesus placed His finger on the very thing the man could not imagine surrendering.
And the man went away sorrowful.
He wanted eternal life.
But when following Jesus threatened the treasure he loved most, he walked away.
That is the tragedy.
He stood before the greatest Treasure in the universe…
And chose what he could not bear to lose.
Now ask yourself something.
If Jesus confronted the one thing you are most afraid to surrender, what would it be?
Your money?
Your image?
Your independence?
Your relationship?
Your secret pleasure?
Your need to control everything?
Your right to remain angry?
What would make you walk away sorrowful?
Be careful before answering.
Because sometimes our idols are not the things we openly worship.
They are the things we quietly refuse to surrender.
And yet, even here, the Gospel shines.
Jesus did not expose that man's attachment because He enjoyed humiliating him.
Scripture tells us Jesus loved him.
The call to surrender was not cruelty.
It was an invitation to freedom.
The same is true when the Word of God exposes us today.
Christ does not reveal sin so that we will despair of His mercy.
He reveals the truth so that we will stop trusting what cannot save us.
And there is something else we must understand.
You are not saved because you have surrendered perfectly. You are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
The original Greek uses the word χάριτί (chariti), from χάρις (charis), meaning grace.
Grace is not a wage you earn after becoming obedient enough.
It is God's undeserved favor.
Salvation is His gift.
You cannot purchase it through good deeds.
You cannot achieve it through religious performance.
You cannot make yourself worthy by collecting enough victories over temptation.
Jesus Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves through His sinless life, sacrificial death, and victorious resurrection.
But the passage does not end at verse nine.
Ephesians 2:10 says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God prepared for us to walk in.
Do you see the beautiful order?
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for a life that bears their fruit.
Obedience is not the price of salvation.
It is a fitting response to the Savior who has redeemed us.
And this is where many people misunderstand the Lordship of Christ.
They hear the call to obedience and immediately imagine a cruel master waiting to reject them after their next failure.
But that is not the Jesus revealed in the Gospel.
He is holy, yes.
He commands repentance, yes.
He calls His disciples to deny themselves, yes.
But He is also the Savior who welcomed sinners, touched the unclean, restored the broken, and gave His life for people who could never save themselves.
Consider Peter.
Peter loved Jesus.
Peter boldly promised loyalty.
He was convinced that even if others fell away, he would remain faithful.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denial.
Three times, Peter denied knowing the Lord he had promised never to abandon.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine the weight of that moment.
Peter had not merely broken a rule.
He had denied his Lord.
The man who had walked on water at Jesus' invitation now stood drowning in shame.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of shame.
You promised God you would never go back.
And you went back.
You cried at the altar.
Then returned to the same compromise.
You said you were finished with the old life.
But somehow the old life found its way into your decisions again.
And now you wonder whether Jesus is tired of hearing your apologies.
But Peter's story did not end in the courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, beside the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus questioned Peter's love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The disciple who had denied Him was not beyond restoration.
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
But Christ's mercy was real too.
And restoration did not mean Peter could simply return to life as though Jesus had no claim over him.
Jesus called him to love, serve, and follow.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain enslaved to the past.
Powerful mercy that brings us back to the One who makes us new.
There is another Greek word worth understanding.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus announces:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — KJV
The word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), from μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It calls for a change of mind and heart, a turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed because you were caught.
More than crying because your choices finally brought consequences.
More than saying “sorry” while secretly planning to continue.
Repentance means coming into agreement with God about sin and turning toward Him.
It does not mean that every temptation instantly disappears.
It does not mean that every wounded habit is healed overnight.
It does not mean a Christian will never fall again.
But it does mean we stop calling darkness light simply because darkness has become familiar.
It means we stop demanding that Jesus bless the very things from which He is calling us to turn.
And it means that when we fall, we do not have to hide from the Savior who calls us back.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is hope for the person who is tired of pretending.
Hope for the believer who has grown spiritually cold.
Hope for the person who has been living two lives.
Hope for the one who is ashamed to admit how far they have wandered.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Maybe you are reading this with tears forming in your eyes.
Maybe you are thinking about the person you have become behind closed doors.
Maybe you remember when prayer was not a routine but a lifeline.
When opening the Bible was not another obligation but a hunger.
When worship was not something you performed for other people but an honest response to the goodness of God.
And somewhere along the way, you became busy.
Distracted.
Comfortable.
Compromised.
You still believed in Jesus.
But you slowly stopped listening to Him.
And now these words are reaching places in your heart that you have kept locked for years.
Please hear this carefully.
Conviction is not the same as condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Those who belong to Christ are not living under the final sentence of condemnation.
Yet the same chapter speaks of putting to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit (Romans 8:13).
Grace does not eliminate the seriousness of sin.
Grace brings us into a new relationship with God, in which the Holy Spirit works to transform us.
The enemy would love for you to confuse conviction with hopelessness.
To believe that because you have failed, you might as well stop fighting.
To believe that because you have fallen repeatedly, returning to Christ is pointless.
But the Gospel calls you to neither denial nor despair.
It calls you to Jesus.
Not to a carefully edited version of yourself.
Not to a performance of spiritual perfection.
To Jesus.
With your sin confessed.
Your pride laid down.
Your excuses abandoned.
Your empty hands open.
There is a sentence from Jesus that may be one of the most challenging invitations ever spoken.
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23, KJV
The Greek word translated “daily” is καθ’ ἡμέραν (kath' hēmeran).
Daily.
Not once during an emotional worship service.
Not only when life becomes unbearable.
Not only when you need a miracle.
Daily.
When the alarm rings and nobody is watching.
When you have an opportunity to retaliate.
When telling the truth could cost you something.
When temptation offers relief without obedience.
When forgiveness feels impossible.
When following Jesus makes you unpopular.
When doing what is right means losing what you wanted.
The cross was not a fashionable religious accessory to Jesus' first hearers.
It was an instrument of execution, associated with suffering, shame, and death.
So when Jesus called people to take up their cross, He was not promising a comfortable life with occasional religious inconvenience.
He was calling them to costly discipleship.
A life no longer centered on self-rule.
But do not misunderstand the invitation.
Jesus is not asking you to suffer in order to prove that His sacrifice was insufficient.
His sacrifice is sufficient.
He calls you to follow because He is worthy, because His way is true, and because the life He gives is greater than the false promises of sin.
The question is not whether following Jesus will cost you something.
It will.
The question is whether you believe He is worth more than what you must leave behind.
Think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
She stood accused, publicly exposed, surrounded by people ready to condemn her.
Jesus confronted the hypocrisy of her accusers, and they departed.
Then He said:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Notice the two truths held together.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy and holiness.
Compassion and truth.
Grace and transformation.
Jesus did not join the crowd in condemning her.
But neither did He declare that sin no longer mattered.
He extended mercy and called her away from the life that had brought her there.
That is the heart of the Gospel we must never distort.
We must not turn Jesus into a merciless judge who refuses to receive repentant sinners.
And we must not reduce Him to a comforting religious figure who never challenges our desires.
He is Savior and Lord.
The Lamb of God who takes away sin.
The risen King to whom all authority belongs.
Philippians 2:9–11 declares that God highly exalted Jesus, and that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
The word κύριος (kyrios) appears again.
Lord.
Not merely an adviser.
Not a spiritual accessory.
Not someone we consult only after our plans fall apart.
Lord.
And one day, every knee will bow.
But today, the invitation is to bow willingly in faith, repentance, and love.
Not because we can earn His acceptance through surrender.
But because the crucified and risen Christ is worthy of our whole lives.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to make Christianity fit around your preferences.
You want peace without repentance.
Blessing without obedience.
Forgiveness without confession.
A crown without a cross.
A Savior who rescues you from judgment, but not a Lord who challenges the throne of your heart.
And yet, there is no greater freedom than belonging to Jesus Christ.
The world tells you freedom means doing whatever you want.
Jesus teaches that sin itself can become slavery.
John 8:34 says:
“Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
And John 8:36 declares:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
What if the very thing you are afraid to surrender is the thing that has been holding you captive?
What if obedience is not the loss of your freedom but the beginning of freedom you have never truly known?
What if the Lordship of Jesus is not the end of your joy but the beginning of a joy no temporary pleasure could ever provide?
You do not need a weaker Jesus who approves everything you do.
You need the real Jesus who loves you enough to tell you the truth.
The Jesus who died for sinners.
The Jesus who rose from the grave.
The Jesus who welcomes the weary.
The Jesus who calls the proud to humility.
The Jesus who forgives the repentant.
The Jesus who restores the fallen.
The Jesus who transforms lives through His Spirit.
The Jesus who says, “Follow Me.”
And maybe, right now, you are finally ready to answer.
Not with another promise you intend to forget.
Not with another emotional moment that ends when you close your phone.
But with a genuine turning of your heart toward Christ.
You may not know how to repair everything you have damaged.
You may not know how to break every sinful pattern overnight.
You may not know how to face the consequences of the choices you have made.
But you can begin with the truth.

“Lord Jesus, I have called You my Savior while resisting Your authority in places I did not want You to touch. I have justified things Your Word calls sin. I have confused Your patience with permission. I have wanted Your blessings more than Your presence.
“Forgive me.
“I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I cannot save myself. I need Your mercy, Your righteousness, and Your transforming grace.

“Teach me to follow You. Give me a heart that loves what You love and turns away from what dishonors You. When I fall, draw me back to repentance instead of hiding. When obedience is costly, remind me that You are worthy.
“Jesus, I do not want to merely speak Your name. I want to belong to You.
“Be Lord over every part of my life.
“Amen.”
If those words express the honest desire of your heart, do not treat this moment as the finish line.
Let it be a beginning.
Open your Bible.
Return to prayer.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek forgiveness where you have wronged someone.
Find a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and where you can grow with other believers.
If you are struggling with a destructive pattern, seek trustworthy pastoral guidance and practical accountability.
And when you fail, do not run from Christ.
Run to Him.
Because the Christian life is not sustained by pretending we are strong.
It is sustained by the grace of the Savior who is faithful.
What is the hardest area of your life to surrender to Jesus right now?
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss publicly.
But if this message has brought something into the light, do not immediately bury that conviction beneath another distraction.
You may discover that you are not the only person fighting a battle behind a smile.
Sometimes the first honest words we speak are the beginning of a much-needed conversation about grace, repentance, and healing.
And please, think about someone you know who needs to read this.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to attack with Scripture.
Someone you genuinely love.
A family member who has drifted from faith.
A friend who is secretly struggling.
A believer who knows all the right words but has grown spiritually numb.
Someone who thinks they have wandered too far for Jesus to welcome them back.
One thoughtful share can begin a conversation you never expected.
Because discipleship should not end when an article ends.
It should continue when the phone is put down and the real decisions begin.
We want the person who cannot afford a Christian book to have access to biblical nourishment.
We want the struggling believer to find resources that help them return to Scripture.
We want families, new Christians, and longtime disciples to have opportunities to grow in their understanding of God's Word.
And keeping that mission growing takes time, work, resources, and people who believe it is worth supporting.
It is a voluntary way to partner with the ongoing work of Gospel-centered encouragement, Christian education, and discipleship.

For those who view financial giving as part of their worship, supporting Gospel ministry can be one meaningful expression of generosity. Scripture encourages willing, cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7), and the support of those who labor in Gospel ministry (Galatians 6:6).
Those gifts cannot be bought.
Our salvation was purchased by Christ, not by our donations.
You are still welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep growing in the Word.
Use the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
And above all, keep following Jesus.
It will be lives directed toward Christ, believers strengthened by Scripture, sinners hearing the Gospel, and people learning to walk in the truth.
Your shares can help others discover it.
But only Jesus can save a soul.
And that is why everything must lead back to Him.
Now, before you leave, return to the question that brought you here.
You want Jesus as your Savior.
But do you really want Him as your Lord?
Not the version of Jesus who never interrupts your plans.
Not the version who agrees with everything you already believe.
Not the version who exists merely to make your life easier.
The real Jesus.
The One who told the truth even when people walked away.
The One who washed His disciples' feet.
The One who forgave sinners and confronted hypocrisy.
The One who carried the cross.
The One who rose victorious over death.
The One who is worthy of your trust, obedience, worship, and love.
Will you follow Him when His Word confronts your desires?
Will you trust Him when surrender feels frightening?
Will you come back when you stumble?
Will you let His grace transform you instead of using His grace as an excuse to remain unchanged?
You do not have to pretend that surrender is easy.
You do not have to claim that every battle is already won.
But you do have to reckon with the question Jesus Himself asked:
“Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?”
The question is not meant to leave you staring hopelessly at your failures.
It is meant to direct your eyes toward the Savior who calls you to follow Him.
And there is still mercy for the person who hears His voice today.
Remember Peter.
Remember the rich young ruler.
Remember the woman who stood accused.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
And remember that no amount of religious appearance can replace the life that comes through faith in Jesus Christ.
Your past may be scandalous.
Your failures may be painful.
Your compromises may be difficult to admit.
But your story does not have to end where your sin left you.
In Christ there is forgiveness.
In Christ there is redemption.
In Christ there is new life.
And through the work of His Spirit, there is genuine transformation.

The greatest tragedy would not be discovering that Jesus wanted more than your religious words, but spending your whole life calling Him “Lord” while refusing the grace that was calling you to follow.
